description: 404 Reika Not Found is a Bandung-based team exploring NASA’s Dancing with the SARs challenge. Our city is slowly sinking, and radar from orbit can measure it. We’re using NISAR data to turn invisible ground motion into maps people can act on. We’re learning SAR as we build, so we value curiosity and honest science over hype. Looking for teammates in remote sensing/GIS, Python, data viz, or Earth science. Join us if you like hard problems and good questions.
summary: GPS surveys and radar studies since 2000 have recorded parts of the Bandung Basin in Indonesia sinking, by up to about 23 cm a year at the fastest sites. If you live there and want to know what is happening under your street, you find journal papers written for specialists. AMBLAS takes the newest open radar data, from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission, and turns it into a web map anyone can open. We found 34 NISAR interferograms over the basin in NASA's catalogue, wrote a Python pipeline that converts them into line-of-sight ground motion, and ran it on the first three real pairs, 19 June to 25 July 2026. The first map followed the mountains around the basin, the signature of atmospheric water vapour. A per-pair elevation correction removed that pattern. All four focus areas now sit within the noise, so we claim no subsidence yet. The app lets you switch between both maps, play the change date by date, and read the value and its uncertainty at any point.
details:
Live app: https://dhatawa.github.io/amblas/ · Source code and documentation: https://github.com/dhatawa/amblas


What it does. You open the map, pick a district (Gedebage, Rancaekek, Dayeuhkolot or Cimahi) or click any point, and AMBLAS tells you three things. It shows which NISAR tracks pass overhead, what our first NISAR result shows there with its uncertainty, and what earlier studies reported for that area, with DOIs. Every value carries a plain-language reading and the limits that apply to it.

How it works. The pipeline searches NASA’s Common Metadata Repository and reads NISAR Level-2 GUNW files from the Alaska Satellite Facility, taking only the window over the basin. It then:

  • drops pixels with coherence below 0.30 or unreliable unwrapping
  • subtracts the ionospheric phase screen that NASA supplies with the product
  • converts phase to millimetres along the radar line of sight, using the wavelength read from each file
  • removes the part of the atmospheric delay that follows terrain height, with a per-pair fit against the Copernicus 30 m elevation model that leaves 3 km around each district out of the fit
  • references each pair to the basin median and stacks the pairs of one track

The output is a set of GeoTIFFs, a map overlay and a summary for each district. A static web app reads these files, so the demo needs no server and runs offline.

First result. Track 082, three 12-day pairs, 86% of pixels valid. Uncorrected, the line-of-sight change followed topography: the basin floor moved toward the satellite relative to the surrounding volcanoes, the pattern of atmospheric water vapour rather than ground motion. The elevation fit (−6.7, −12.8 and −41.1 mm per km of height for the three pairs) removed that pattern. The four districts now read between −8.3 and +9.2 mm, each within its own 2σ uncertainty and our 15 mm noise floor. A broad north-south gradient of about 25 mm remains, which we treat as residual atmosphere. At the published average rate for Bandung, 36 days would produce only about 7 mm, so this window is too short to detect subsidence. Our phase sign convention matches MintPy's NISAR reader; we have not yet checked it against GNSS.

Benefits and impact. Residents get one place to read what radar shows about their area and how far to trust it. Researchers get a tested, scripted starting point for NISAR time series over Bandung. Local agencies get a shared reference for deciding where ground surveys would pay off. AMBLAS supports monitoring and decisions. It does not prevent floods or stop subsidence.

Creativity. We pointed L-band data released this year at a problem with twenty years of published research behind it, and we built the app to show uncertainty as clearly as the result. Empty layers stay empty. Simulated test data carries a label. Each district panel separates what NISAR measured from what older papers reported.

Factors we considered. We report line-of-sight change and avoid calling it vertical subsidence, because one viewing direction cannot separate up-down from east-west motion. Four months of data cannot give an annual rate, so we give none. Each granule weighs 2.2 GB, so we processed three of the nine available pairs and wrote a command that crops granules to the basin. Next we plan a weather-model correction for the remaining atmosphere, the other six track-082 pairs, the descending track 090 to separate vertical from horizontal motion, and a comparison with GNSS stations.

Use of AI tools. We used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and writing assistant: to search NASA's catalogue and the literature, write and debug the Python pipeline and web app, draft documentation, and discuss how to read the first result. The team chose the problem, downloaded and processed the NISAR granules on our own machine, reviewed the results and edited the text. No AI-generated data is shown as an observation, and simulated test data is labelled in the app.
